utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we begin today, coming back to the issue you raised, Mr. Tieger, as to the complete witness list for the Prosecution, the Chamber finds it to be helpful to have a complete list of 65 ter list on the part of the Prosecution. Given that since it was filed in 2009, there were several revisions or amendment, but we didn't have one. But the new list, complete list, should not be accompanied with summaries. I don't think that would be very burdensome on your part. And my -- and on a separate issue, whether you had the opportunity to look into the list of funding countries for the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My mistake, Mr. President. I wasn't able to reach Mr. Vanderpuye. I'll do that this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you come back to me after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My apologies for your inconvenience, Ms. Frease. If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Good morning, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Frease.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 90321, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Frease, what I'm going to bring up on the screen in a minute is a witness statement recently signed by you when I arrived here in The Hague. You should see it in a minute. Do you remember going through this statement and signing it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just have a couple questions about it. Could you please confirm for the Trial Chamber that you went through the statement and read it carefully before signing, and that it's accurate?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, I did; and yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And would your answers on the same topics, if you were asked again today, be the same as they are in the statement, not necessarily word for word, but the information you would give would be the same?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be next Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It should be put under seal, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, I was just going to say, Your Honours, we have a public version and a redacted version. And the only reason for it being under seal is it refers to two sites which are not normally mentioned in paragraph 19. And so we have redacted those from the public version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Why don't we give two numbers for both versions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, confidential version of statements shall assigned Exhibit P4647, under seal. And public version shall assigned Exhibit P4648. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would now tender the associated exhibits, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I could just say, Your Honours, in relation to the various intercepts that are in 65 ter 02622, I will talk about some of those intercepts today, not all of them, and show some additional intercepts, and my proposal which I discussed with Mr. Robinson just a moment ago would not be to formally tenderer those all at this time but do it globally later with some others in a motion we're preparing. Or if you're -- the Trial Chamber wishes, of course, we could assign the exhibit numbers now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that it was dealt with in her statement and there's no opposition, the Chamber doesn't see any problem admitting it. But with respect 3402, is there an English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Should we upload it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- is, Your Honours. If I can just check. Yes, there is, Your Honours. The English translation of 3402 is just for the cover sheet, not for the table with all of the numbers. We could provide that, but it's -- at the moment, what we have is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it has been uploaded in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I apologise then, Your Honours. We will upload that, then, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And with respect to 23548, when I read the transcript -- the -- Ms. Frease's statement, I was not sure whether that is the document that was discussed in her statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honours. It is a bit strange-looking, when read with the statement. But we could bring that up right now and show it to Ms. Frease and she can explain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Why don't you do that. And, finally, with respect to 23657, would you not object to the addition to the 65 ter list, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All right. After giving a brief summary of her evidence, why don't you deal with those exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And just before we move on, I should say in reference to 02622 which is the authentication binder, we prepared an index which cross-references have not yet been distributed. It has been uploaded now as the last three pages. I gave copies to my friends and I have hard copy for the Chamber, if the Chamber would like, and it shows the 65 ter numbers and e-court pages for each of the documents in the -- in that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That would be very helpful. So all -- so why don't we deal with the associated exhibits after her evidence in-chief is over.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll now go through a quick witness summary of Ms. Frease's evidence. Ms. Frease joined the OTP Srebrenica investigative team in January 1996. From March 1998 to July 2000, she was involved in the translation, authentication, and analysis of radio intercepts attained by the Office of the Prosecutor. Ms. Frease, in her statement, explained the history of the investigation and the methods used to verify the intercepts' reliability and authenticity. These included comparing and matching different versions of the intercept, handwritten, printouts, electronic, and audio recordings, analysing independent documentation, for example, VRS documents, to see whether or not they corroborated certain specific intercepts, and interviewing intercept operators. The results of these -- time and this work and analysis by Ms. Frease satisfied her that the intercepts were genuine and reliable. And during her time working on this Intercept Project, as it was called, Ms. Frease never found any indication that the intercepts had been fabricated. That concludes of summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, let me now ask you just a couple questions about this intercept project.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The first thing I want to do is just expand a little bit on the statement - excuse me - in paragraph 21 of the statement, it states -- you stated: "In assessing the reliability of the material we had received, we first looked for internal consistency among the documents. What I mean by 'internal consistency,' is that the printouts matched with the notebooks that we received." And my question is simply: Based on that exercise, what was your assessment overall, of the internal consistency, as you called it, between the printouts and the notebooks?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: They were very -- they were very consistent. We started with the printouts, looking at those, and then went to the original source documents, the notebooks, the handwritten notebooks, and saw that they -- they matched; in most cases, identical. Occasionally they were slight time differences that were indicated on the printed material. And that had to do with when the typist typed up the documents, which was sometimes just a couple of minutes after the conversation had been transcribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you. One more question on the statement. Thank you. One more question on the statement. In the next paragraph, 22, we see: "We also received radio intercepted communication data from different sources, namely the military and SDB. We compared the intercepts of the SDB against the intercepts of the army in order to determine whether the same or related conversations were captured at the same time. Our findings in relation to the consistencies between two separate sources of intercept materials were a factor which led us to believe they were reliable." And my question is: If you could just expand on that. What were the findings, if you could describe them, of your comparison between the ABiH intercepts and the state security, SDB, intercepts?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: So, by now, I'm sure the Chamber knows that there were four different units working at two different sites, and three of the units were military units and one was a police unit. And what we found -- so each of them was doing their work independently. What we found when various units recorded the same conversation was that there was internal consistency among the transcriptions of those conversations, so we did not find that there were any substantial differences between the substance of the conversations that the police took down and that the military took down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 24, you describe comparing intercepts to third-party information, such as VRS documents. And I want to look at that process now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 02622, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that is something we've referred to as the intercept authentication binder. And, if I'm correct, that was prepared long ago for testimony in the Krstic case; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's correct. And then parts of it were also used in subsequent trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. There we have the cover page. And you explained in your statement the way this binder works, so I won't go through that now. What I'd like to do is go to talk about, to illustrate the contents, a couple of examples. And the first one is tab 8 which is entitled in the index there, fuel order, an intercept from 16 July 1995 at 1358. So could we go to e-court page 61, please. Now, there, can you tell us this is simply at the beginning of this tab a summary of what the intercept is about?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one question, Mr. Nicholls. Do these individual intercepts have its own 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: They do, in our 65 ter list, Your Honours. I think nearly all of them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For example, how can the Defence find the B/C/S version for this intercept?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's actually included in the binder, in the next -- in the following page. Each intercept in this binder first has the English version and then following the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Handwritten version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Handwritten, or printout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, we'll go through this intercept in a minute. But can you just tell the Chamber briefly, if you remember, why did you select this intercept as an example?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Well, there were a couple of reasons. This intercept for me always stood out because it was the first one that we identified when we were working on the collection in the field in 1998 where we were working with the -- with the printout material, and it was the first conversation where we were able to put a date and some details to activity that we knew about independently that had come from an insider who had been at Pilice farm at the time that executions were being conducted. So that stands out to me about this intercept. But then we were able to also corroborate it through seized documents from the VRS, from the Zvornik Brigade, and I guess we'll look at that document in a moment, but it was a fuel order that then substantiated it. So it was a good example, a good illustration of how we could independently corroborate the veracity of the intercepted communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, right at the top, we see Zlatar and then duty officer and Palma and then duty officer, so a conversation between two duty officers. Can you tell us, if you remember, what Zlatar stands for and then what Palma stands for?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, Zlatar was the code-name of the Drina Corps based in Vlasenica, and Palma was the code-name of the Zvornik Brigade based in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then, just briefly, could we have 65 ter 03442, and then I'll come back to this intercept.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's -- excuse me, there's a typo on line 13 that says -- it is supposed to say "Zlatar," Z-l-a-t-a-r.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now this is a VRS code-name chart. And, actually, with we had put in an updated version which is not the one in there, so I will try to change that later. But can you just tell us about what this code-name chart is and how it was used by the team?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: So, it was put together to -- as a guide for the team to be able to understand the meaning of the intercepts. It's really, I think, pretty straightforward, goes with the code-name, panorama. That was comes up a lot in the intercepted communication, and that was the code-name for the VRS Main Staff. A couple of the others -- I'll list three of the others that came up a lot in the communication: Zlatar, the Drina Corps; Palma, the Zvornik Brigade; and Badem, which was the Bratunac Brigade. And then the others relate to other military units and the code-names associated with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender that document, Your Honours, with the caveat that we have a slightly more updated version which was not in e-court yet, by accident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of this 3442?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- as Exhibit P4649. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. If we could go back to the intercept we were looking at now on 65 ter 02622, page 62. Well, while we're waiting for it to come up on the screen, to save time, I'll just read out the points I was going to point to you. We'll see when this comes up that the Zlatar duty officer is speaking with the Palma duty officer. And the Palma or Zvornik Brigade duty officer says: "500 litres of D-2 diesel fuel for Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic." And then further down --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you wait until it appears in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just before we go to the fuel log you spoke about, can we see here that in this series of four conversations which are broken up, that the discussion is about Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic needing 500 litres of D-2 fuel, otherwise his work will stop, to summarise?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if we look --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Can this be blown up on my screen a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. And if we can blow up the background portion, please. And we see here that Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic is here at Palma at the time?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd now like to go to e-court page 66, a few pages down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now here just so we can see how your binder works, could you just explain what this is, this next cover sheet, saying: corroborating material.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It's a summary of the fuel receipt that we seized under search-warrant from the Zvornik Brigade headquarters in 1998, and the receipt specifies 500 litres of D-2 fuel that was issued to Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic on the 16th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we go to the next page, please. This is the translation of the fuel log. The original is on the next page if anybody needs to see it. And here we see this fuel log at the top has the date 16 July 1995. In box 15, we see "for Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic." I should have said that on the top left we see: material list for dispatch. And if we scroll -- well, we can see it, actually, below, that the material is diesel fuel, D-2, requested, approved, 500. Signed by, we see the signature, Sretan Milosevic. I think it is pretty clear, but can you tell us why, how you picked this to corroborate the intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Because it speaks very -- it speaks to some very specific items. The dates correspond, to begin with, on the 16th of July. This is coming from the Zvornik Brigade, so from Palma. It's issued to Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic who is also mentioned in the intercept. It mentions specifically D-2. It mentions 500 litres. So these are all very specific items that can be matched to the radio intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to show you a related document that's not in the binder. That's the Zvornik Brigade duty officer notebook, P04585. Page 148, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It should be page 148 in both the English and the original. Okay. If we could blow it up a bit, for the English, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now we just discussed that Palma was the Zvornik Brigade and went through the intercept at 1358 with the duty officer speaking. This is the duty officer notebook of the Zvornik Brigade from the same day, 16 July. I'll read out the entry at 1400. It states: "At 1400 hours, Popovic requested a bus with a full tank of 500 litres of D-2 diesel. Zlatar duty officer and Golic informed." So very simply, this isn't in the binder, but how does this fit in with the intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It reinforces the intercept further. The time is indicated there, so the intercept was recorded at 1358, and this entry indicates a conversation taking place at 1400 hours, whereby Popovic, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, is requesting 500 litres of D-2 fuel. It mentions the Zlatar duty officer and Golic. Golic was the security officer at Zlatar, and his name was also mentioned in the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could go back to the binder now. 02622. Go through one more example.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when that comes up, I'd like to go to page 46, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, Ms. Frease, we'll be discussing tab 6 of the binder which is an intercepted conversation dated 13 July 1995. It's actually two conversations, one at 1602 and one at 1730. Now, again, we'll go through the documents, but could you tell the Chamber what it was that made you pick this example as one for inclusion in your binder of examples of the type of work that you did to corroborate the intercepts?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Well, they were conversations that discussed the fact that Muslim men were being gathered at a soccer field or a soccer pitch in Nova Kasaba on the 13th of July in the afternoon. So pretty specific information. It provided a location and the type of -- and the type of location, it being a soccer field, so it was something that we felt we could corroborate with other information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next page, please, and look at the first intercept from 1602. And could you just tell us about this intercept, which speaks about an extension down in Kasaba where Malinic's unit is. 1500 gathered at the stadium, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, so this conversation takes place on the 13th of July. We were able to date it through the dating system that we went through in the work. It mentions here Kasaba. It mentions Malinic's unit, Zoran Malinic. We know Malinic's unit to have been Zoran Malinic's unit. He was the head of the MP Unit for the 65th Protection Regiment that was based in Nova Kasaba. It mentions that there are over 1500 - I would say people - gathered at the stadium and those are the identifying features of that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could skip ahead two pages now to the next intercept you included from the same day at 1730 hours. And we see here that it begins talking about asking for ten buses from Bijeljina: "Well, tell them right away to come down. There's about 6.000 of them now. X participant says that: "Of military age." And Y says: "Shut up. Don't repeat." And then continues to talk about whether women and children are still being transported. And further down, just where we are now: "So I am to send," something is missing, "and have them report on Kasaba, have them report to the stadium." Can you just tell us quickly about this intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I think it has been summarised fairly well. But earlier in the intercept it also mentions about 1500 to 2.000 people, roughly, having been collected at three points. It mentions Kasaba again. It mentions the stadium, and the stadium can mean a soccer pitch in Kasaba. It was also recorded on the 13th of July, an hour and a half after the -- after the other one. So those were fairly unique features.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] okay. If we could go to page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise. If we could go to page 54 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And here it just tells that part of -- well, the corroborating material you selected is an aerial image; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we turn the page and see that image, if you could tell us how that correlates to the intercepts we saw.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: So this was aerial imagery that the team received, and the analyst who worked on this identified the blocks, or circles, I guess. Well, there are blocks of individuals with circles around them indicating that there are groups of prisoners there. The overhead imagery was dated on 13 July at about 2.00 in the afternoon. And the soccer pitch is mentioned, the football field, in Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to -- staying on this particular -- particular topic, look at a couple of more intercepts that are not in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 31000, please. This is an intercept also from 13 July at 1400. I don't think that's the right one. 31000. Okay. I need the English, actually, which -- let's try... okay. There we go. If we could blow up the English please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it correct? I can't find it. But we have it in front of us. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, A, sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So here we have -- this is 13 July -- if we scroll up to the top, we can see at 1400. At frequency 254.300. We don't know the names of the participants. It says X and Y. We see down at the second line: "I have more than a thousand. "Where are they?" Looking down further: "Down at the football stadium." And then we see: "All of them, man, all are able-bodied. "I don't know whether to give these to them. "To whom? "To Zoka and the other one." Is Zoka a nickname? You can tell us what that means.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Zoka is a nickname for Zoran, and in this context would refer to Zoran Malinic, again, the head of the Military Police Battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment that was based in Kasaba on the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Again this is dated -- timed at 1400 on 13 July. Is that the same time as the aerial we saw?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's correct. And this one says there are more than a thousand, as you had read.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I now go to 31007, please. C, I think will work. If we could have the English as well, please. No, that's not the right one. It should be 3100 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it may be A.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, try A, please. 31007A. Yes. That's it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this intercept is from five minutes later on the same frequency, 254.300 on the same day. And we see the two participants X and Y saying: "Where is that? "Here at the football pitch. "Is it visible? "Fuck, it is. "Brother, don't take anyone. I'll send you an urgent telegram now. Don't take anyone. I'll send you a telegram now and explain it to you. "... "Secure it well and you'll get it now in the telegram." Can you tell us about this intercept, if you can make any connection to it, same frequency, five minutes later, from the last one?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, on this one, there's less obvious information until we look at a subsequent document, but here we see again the football pitch being mentioned. The time of day, as you mentioned, 1405, on the 13th of July, and then -- I mean, it mentions an urgent telegram that I think we'll look at next.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could now have P00168.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just see the bottom of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: P00168, please. And this is a document headed IKM of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment, Borike, at 1400 hours. It is dated 13 July 1995 in handwriting on the bottom. And it is typed signed from commander Lieutenant-Colonel Milomir Savcic. Do you know who Milomir Savcic was in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, he was the commander of the 65th Protection Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's just go through this document a bit. This is the one where you explained that the last intercept we were looking at related to a document you thought we would see in a minute. If we could go now to the first page in the English, please. This is headed: Procedure for treatment of war prisoners to the commander of the Main Staff for information to the assistant commander for morale, religious and legal affairs of the Main Staff and commander of the Military Police Battalion of the 6th Protection Regiment. And you said that was Zoran Malinic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. How does this document relate to the intercept, in your view?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Okay. So, it relates because it is coming from the commander of the 65th Protection Regiment. It's going to his deputy, Zoran Malinic, who is mentioned in a couple of the intercepts and who is located in Kasaba. This order states that there are over a thousand members of the former 28th Division of the so-called Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina captured in the area of Dusanovo which is also known as Kasaba. The prisoners are under the control of the Military Police Battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment. So all of that information confirms what we -- what was recorded in the radio intercepts that we saw earlier. It goes on to say that the assistant commander of the security and intelligence affairs of the General Staff of the VRS, who was General Tolimir, proposes the following. And then it goes through a few points like prohibiting access to unauthorised individuals, prohibiting traffic for all UN vehicles, and then it says that the commander of the Military Police Battalion shall take measures to remove war prisoners from the main Milici-Zvornik road and place them indoors in the area protected from sighting from the ground or the air. There is a fourth point on the next page ... Okay. Which isn't directly related to the radio intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And just looking at the intercept we saw previously, 31007, do you recall that in that one of -- intercept one of the interlocutors was asking whether they were -- whether it is visible?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Could you say what time that -- yes, I do remember that -- that it was. But I --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That was at 1405.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Uh-huh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Those are the only examples I want to go through because of the timing of this binder you put together. And you referred to tab 1 and explained it in the statement that's been admitted. But I want to ask you: Based on the type of analysis we've just seen here, you explaining in the courtroom, and what you explain in your statement, in the time you worked on the Intercept Project, which I believe was a little bit over two years, in the end, what was your assessment, based on all the work you did, on the authenticity of the intercepts the OTP received?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: My assessment was that the intercepts were both authentic and reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, do you tender those two additional intercepts we dealt with just now, 31000A and 31007A?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but just, really, whichever the Court wishes. I can either tender them now or as part of a -- a larger solution. We will be filing a motion with various intercepts on it and we can refer to this testimony in that motion. But, really, whichever the Court feels is most useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With respect to those two item, I take it there are no objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we add them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Give a number for those two.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 31000A shall be assigned P4670, and 65 ter 31007A shall be assigned Exhibit P4671. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can we correct the transcript at line 8, 20.8. My assessment was that the intercepts were both authentic and reliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Rest assured, they will be corrected in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I come back to the associated exhibits. You said you would deal with 23548 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- and I would like you to also deal with 23657 as well for the same reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Your Honours, I forgot that. You're correct. 23548, if I could have that, please. And we need the English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Frease, these two documents are referred in paragraph 5 of your amalgamated statement which reads: "The first material we received, in March 1998, consisted of approximately 550 pages of printouts of ABiH intercepts ..." and that the documents with 65 ter numbers 23548 and 23657 record this transfer.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you tell us what -- we have now have 23548 on the screen, could you tell us how this related to this first batch of 550 intercepts -- pages of intercepts?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: This was the receipt that Jean-Rene Ruez, the team leader for the Srebrenica investigation, signed when he took possession of that binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And if we go to the next page, and then maybe the next page. On the back of this receipt, there was included some information on the charts on the structure of the Drina Corps, is that right, that this was included on top of the package of printouts?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. Along with it, mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have the next document. 23657, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand this doesn't really look like a receipt. But can you tell us what this document had to do with the -- with that batch of intercepts received by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It was the cover sheet located inside the binder of 550 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's what I would have on those two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. So including 2622, we will admit them all and be -- the numbers would be given in due course by the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I note that one of the associated exhibits, i.e., 30921, was already admitted when KDZ357 was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Madam Frease.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I should like to begin with what is the freshest on our minds, but I need to know, with your leave, how well you know the Serbian language and how did you acquire that knowledge? Where did you study?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I would say that I have a good working knowledge of the language. Regrettably, I would say that I never really studied it. I picked it up along the way, and primarily when I worked in Bosnia during the war, and then more when I worked for the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you have no roots in the former Yugoslavia, do you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I do have roots in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you tell us what kind, although you don't have to, if you mind?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I have one set of grandparents who are from the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know the meaning of the word "zacepiti," "to plug"?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Which is one of the meanings, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that it is -- it means to cork a bottle or to use something to -- to plug something, to close it.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, that's my familiarity with that word.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you tell the Trial Chamber what the opposite concept would be? How would you call the opposite action?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: So "odcepiti."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this transcript, it could have been P5470, 65 ter 31000 formally, that word remained untranslated. Do you remember the passage where it says "term unknown"? Shall we call it again, or do you remember?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I do remember it. And I wondered why it hadn't been translated, actually. But those were not my translations; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. But what I want to know is what would be the result of your work. Is it just a verification of the accuracy of the transcription, or it had broader implications, as in the case with fuel. In other words, did you use everything that could corroborate an intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I used my language skills to go over the translations quite a bit with translators and language assistants. I would say that that was a fairly small part of my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this question, I did not refer to language. For example, the number 1500 and over 1500 is mentioned and repeated. And you mentioned that the analyst had identified footage that -- or, rather, recordings that corroborate the content of this analysis. This number, 1500 or over 1.000, is it accurate?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That was based on information that the VRS was providing to its command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you did not check whether that fighter -- or, rather, huntsman exaggerated. Do you know what I mean by hunting tales?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, in our language, when you say "hunting tales," you mean exaggeration of one's catch. Tall tales, in other words. When you were learning our language, did you come across that idiom, "hunting tales"?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I don't remember that specifically. But to your point about whether the numbers were exaggerated between 1.000 and 1500, if those were -- those numbers came from soldiers who were on the ground who had responsibility for guarding prisoners. There were also bus loads of people who were being transported out of the enclave who saw many, many, many people gathered on that football stadium. So those specific accounts that VRS soldiers reported in their communications, I believe, would have had to have been accurate because they needed to worry about security of those prisoners and also transportation of those prisoners, knowing how many buses to get in order to move the prisoners. So, I mean, that information came from the Bosnian Serb side. We also had independent corroboration from people who were being transported out of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. No objection. I just wanted, for the record, I didn't know who Mr. Karadzic was referring to as the huntsman or the person who exaggeration. Is that Lieutenant-Colonel Milomir Savcic of the document we saw, or is he referring to one of the interlocutors in the intercept?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think she answered the question, so let's proceed. Or would you like to clarify Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this opportunity to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Savcic, too, receives reports from the ground. The one who took prisoners says he caught over 1.000 up to 1500. So those people who took prisoners report how many there are. And my question has to do with the fact that Ms. Frease says the analyst also analysed this photograph in order to corroborate intercepts. I want to know whether he also analysed the number that features there, or the numbers were taken as in disputable.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I'm not aware the analyst provided a number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we then look at -- I believe it's page 55 because 54 was the transcript, and the next page is the photo. Number 622, the one we looked at. Thank you. Could we see this pitch full screen. I meant the pitch alone. If we could zoom in. Could we zoom in further, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, Ms. Frease, that we can see individuals here, both those standing in front of the group in the rectangle and since they are standing, their shadows are a bit thinner, and the people sitting?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that on the left we can't see they are lined in two rows, and we can see every individual?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's correct. That's what I'm saying. And part of the reason that I'm saying that is that I have never analysed overhead imagery so I don't know what a dot represents. But I do also remember an intercept from 1009 on the morning of the 13th, between Colonel Beara, Zoka and Lucic, who had been Zoka's deputy, in which they took about, I think Beara, Colonel Beara, is giving an order to line them up in four or five rows. There's also reference to: Are there big heads there? They are trying to separate possibly some of the leaders of the BiH division. So I don't know. Maybe -- maybe on the left side which you're look at is people who are lined up in four or five rows, also prisoners - that would be, I don't know, possible - and this other group, a much larger group of other prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know the size of a football field, I mean the European kind of football?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I cannot give you dimensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that it's 80 by 40, and the largest ones are 100 by 50, does that sound acceptable to you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I don't know the dimensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Can we agree that this larger group of people lined in five rows occupies a small portion of the field?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I can't agree with your statement that the larger group occupies four or five rows.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, how many rows would this larger group be lined in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm wondering if this witness is a best suited witness to deal with the aerial image. I am of the impression that we're wasting time. You have another opportunity to deal with it. And I think we have better image for this -- for this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I mean, the witness has already said she has no expertise in analysing overhead imagery. So, in effect, you are asking her to guess or to agree with a guess, which is not very satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, do you have a 65 ter number for page 28 of Jean-Rene Ruez's book?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes it's P4308, probably e-court page 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, what I want to know is: What was the approach of your team that analyses and runs checks on additional information that could be corroborative? Did you also check things that could be favourable to the Serbian side; in other words, to the truth?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: We were very careful in the analysis that we conducted. From the very beginning, we approached this material with skepticism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. For the Registrar, it is 65 ter 3199, page 38. Please continue, Ms. Frease.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We took the approach that the material was fabricated, and it was up to us to figure out whether or not it was. We undertook a very meticulous analysis of every piece of information that related to the intercepted material. This included, as my statement says and I've testified before, analysing the printed binder, comparing that to the notebooks, the handwritten notebooks where the radio intercept operators transcribed the conversations. It then involved comparing those conversations, finding overlapping conversations that were taken from two sites and multiple units and comparing the consistency and professionalism with which the ABiH allegedly did this work. It then involved lengthy conversations with the intercept operators. That was all to test the reliability and the authenticity of the material. In the process of doing that and because I had been involved with the investigation early on and the investigative team was constantly working with new material, material that had been seized from the VRS and other material; for example, letters that -- of notes -- sorry. Not letters, but notes that had been transcribed from conversations between VRS military and UNPROFOR generals. We cast the net as widely as we could to corroborate various conversations through many different sources. So we arrived at the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's precisely what I am interested in. Did you check whether it was recorded accurately and accurately transcribed what the speakers were saying, or did you also check whether they were telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: We checked both.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your team then accept that there are over 1.000 people on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I'm not an analyst of aerial imagery, but this photograph represented -- corroborated information that had been transmitted in about five intercepted conversations from that day, starting from 10.09 in the morning until 1730 in the afternoon, but two in particular from 2.00 p.m. and 2.05 p.m. along with a telegram from Milomir Savcic whose unit was responsible for securing prisoners at Nova Kasaba on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it indisputable that Savcic was not on the ground? He was sending instructions to people on the ground. Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: He was in Borike. He was close by, yes. And he was relying on his people on the ground to give him information about what was happening; his deputy, in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So this photograph was taken sometime around 1400 hours on the 14th [as interpreted] July and the intercept, speaking about over 1.000 prisoners on the football field dates back to the same time. Did you check whether they were telling the truth? Not necessarily you. You had your own analysts. You said, on page 14, that you had an analyst who analysed the photograph to corroborate the intercept.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: So, one small correction. It was on the 13th of July at 1400 hours. I guess you're saying that -- that the -- that Zoran Malinic and others on the ground from those five intercepts were lying on the 13th, and what we know from the facts based on, again, people driving by in buses who were being deported from the -- from the enclave or evacuated from the enclave were that there were many, many, many people on the field in Nova Kasaba. I cannot say any -- I cannot give you a number. I cannot put a number to the -- to how many people were photographed in this aerial image.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe you have agreed that you did not only check whether the recording and transcription were done accurately, but you also check whether they relate to an accurate, to a real event. Did your team accept that there were more than 1.000 prisoners on the football field?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: She answered the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure I have the answer, that after all the checks, all the verifications, the conclusion of the team was that, indeed, there were 1.000 prisoners on the stadium. The witness did not confirm this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The VRS people who were on the ground at the time estimated that the number of people who were on the field at that time was between 1.000 and 1500 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question was whether the OTP team had the conclusion as to the number, which is shown at this picture.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that we accepted the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this simultaneous photograph, or, rather, contemporaneous photograph, support this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That one, I think, Your Honour, has been asked over and over again, about whether the numbers on the photo go with the intercept, and she's answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's the answer she gave.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You, or somebody else maybe, made a selection of intercepts. What were your guide-lines in selecting intercepts? From what viewpoint did you choose them? From the viewpoint of the OTP, or from the viewpoint of justice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but what does that mean, selected intercepts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could you clarify, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 8 of today's transcript, Ms. Frease said they were guided by certain considerations - let's find that page -- by certain reasons and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, did you mean the selection in the course of producing authentication binder, which is 65 ter number 2622.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Your Excellencies, that they made a selection and that not all intercepts were presented to this court. We see -- we see that out of 4.000 intercepts of my conversations, the Bosnian side provided only 1.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'll find the passage in page 8.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 17 on page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was related specifically to the binder where I asked, Why did you select this particular document as an example for this particular exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then my question is: Did you make a selection; and, if so, what kind? Or you presented all the intercepts you could get a hold of?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: We analysed all of the intercepts that we got a hold of. We worked from the front cover of one notebook to the back cover of every notebook and processed all of the intercepts. The ones that have been selected for court are ones that are relevant to a particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I'm asking. From what standpoint? From the standpoint of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's certainly not for this witness to explain what intercepts the Prosecutors, the attorneys, decided to put on the 65 ter list in a particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. But in previous answers, she said the ones that have been selected for court, the ones that are relevant to a particular case. So the question -- I took the question to mean that whether she was involved in that selection, per case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you bring to the Prosecution all the intercepts, or you made a selection before submitting them to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I was always working for the OTP, so the material came in to the OTP, and we then processed it. Initially, I think, when the notebooks were first identified, I believe that members of the OTP - I was not among them - but they made a selection of the notebooks based on certain dates. But then that -- the breadth or the range of dates expanded, and as we received more material, we processed it all. We were very interested in knowing that the information that we had was factually correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if it is convenient.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question. Just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You've mentioned earlier today five intercepts in those critical hours. Did you show just two or three instead of all five? Could we perhaps see all five of them?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: We showed four, and maybe I shouldn't have mentioned the fifth. I mean, it was at 10.09 in the morning. It was just something that I remembered for having worked on them for a long time. But it relates to prisoners being held on the soccer pitch on 13th of July. And, at that time, at 10.09 in the morning, they estimated that there were about 400 prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, just if -- that's 30980A, I believe, the intercept being referred to, if Mr. Karadzic wants to look it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you see that 400 and 1500 is a big difference. This is much closer to the photograph, wouldn't you agree, Ms. Frease? It's much closer to the photograph, although it's still too much.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Again, I'm not an analyst of aerial imagery. This intercept was taken at the 10.09 in the morning. The photograph was taken at 2.00 in the afternoon. There are two other intercepts and a military document from Milomir Savcic that talk about there being a thousand to 1500 prisoners on the soccer pitch at 2.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say aerial image was taken at what time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At 2.00 in the afternoon, 1400.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not up to 2.00? It says dash or something like that. Shall we zoom out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately 2.00 in the afternoon. That squiggle is approximate; yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take a break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd also like to tender that transcript, the one that speaks about 400, although I have reservations where transcripts are concerned, generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All right. Let's take a -- what is the number, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 30980A. And no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, why were you not supposed to mention the fifth?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It's not that I wasn't supposed to mention the fifth. We didn't think it was as relevant to the particular document and to the timing of the aerial image. I have no problem with 10.09 in the morning. It -- it's all -- it's all about the same subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 16 on page 34 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2204, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give the number again. D ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D2204. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one final question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Line 16, page 36, you said: Perhaps I shouldn't have mentioned the fifth. Now, don't you think that it is very relevant for the Defence that you should mention this fifth one? So are you being a bit selective here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: She answered -- she answered the question, didn't she?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then we can go on break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I leave it to the parties and Registry whether we need to admit in redacted version or put under seal, as regards the intercepts. We will take a break for half an hour, and we will resume at 11.05.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Robinson, we received a file, both in -- both confidential and public redacted version, from the UK government for -- asking for a further extension. Do you have any observation, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We don't object to that but we would ask that this be the last extension that they receive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That is helpful. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I just wanted to say that the code-name sheet, 65 ter 03442, the correct version has now been uploaded, and the English translation of 65 ter 03402 has now been uploaded. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you seek to obtain intercepts from the Serb side in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that decision taken by the team, or were you advised by the OTP that you shouldn't do it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I really don't remember, but I think that we just didn't think we would get anything from the Serb side. I mean, I certainly was not advised not to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the Republika Srpska government received the investigators of the OTP in December 1996 and in January 1997 and provided the documents they had and subsequently they provided everything that they -- that was sought from them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't want to make an argument in front of the witness about that. But based on the record -- I'm not sure that's a fair question, I'll say that, based on the record in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Ms. Frease, what I would like to know is: Where did that presumption that the Serbs would not co-operate come from; especially so as at the time my political opponents were, in fact, in power?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether she said that Serb side would not co-operate. But, in any event, you can -- you can answer the question, Ms. Frease.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lines 21 and 22 on page 37: [In English] "... we just didn't think we would get anything from the Serb side."

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: In the context, in 1998, February -- I think it was February of 1998, we conducted the search warrants in Bratunac and Zvornik. The situation was still quite hostile in Republika Srpska with respect to the Office of the Prosecutor and the ICTY. When we conducted investigations in Republika Srpska, starting in the spring of 1996, to identify the sites of executions and detention centres for prisoners, we required a lot of physical protection. And, again, the situation on the ground was quite hostile. In -- in March of 1998, when we received the first intercepted communication from the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it took us some time - over a year, I would say - to work through that information and to determine whether it was authentic or reliable. So it was just in the context of the ongoing investigation that we -- to my knowledge, we did not forward a RFA, or Request for Assistance, to Bosnian Serbs for radio intercepted communication that they would have taken of their own communication during the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Just a month before you were there, the investigators went to see some members of the government. Is it your position that the government, too - in other words, the central authorities - were as suspicious and restrictive, or wary, as the people on the ground where there might have been some perpetrators who were then wary for that reason?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It was not an easy situation at the time on the side of the government or the side of individuals. That's my impression and memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you investigate the war-time events, or, rather, the war crimes, or was it, in fact, the conduct of the Serb side that was the subject of your investigation?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: War crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, do you think, then, that the Serbs would fail to mention something that they could about their opponents in the war?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I did not personally have much contact with ... the Serbs during the war -- or, sorry, in the post-war period. So I guess it would have been the Serbs' responsibility to provide that information to the OTP. I, however, had been assigned to the Srebrenica investigation, so that was where my focus was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And as part of that investigation, you focussed on the conduct of the Serb side alone; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What time-frame of Srebrenica did you investigate?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I was particularly focussed on the events immediately following the fall of the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you concluded or observed that the Muslim side, too, was reserved and that they did not hand over the intercepts when expected in 1995, but, rather, only later in 1998?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's correct that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina handed over the intercepts in 1998. We -- in 1995, in July of 1995, I was a part of the initial team that went out to Tuzla, and we established immediate contact with the police of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Tuzla. So we did establish that immediate contact in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you were aware, weren't you, that in those three years, there was a possibility of alterations or fabrications; in other words, that those intercepts could have been fabricated but let's not limit ourselves to that. They could have also been altered. Did you take that into account?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any knowledge or did you assume that the Muslim side would be selective and that they would try to conceal some matters that would be favourable to the Serb army or the Serb side, or that they would conceal something that would be at the expense of the Serb side? So if a selection was made, which of these two scenarios do you see as more likely?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, we considered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive information that was certain about what had happened to the audio material, and were you provided the entire collection of the audio recordings?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: We always asked for all of the information in its original form, not any analysis that would have been done by the ABiH or the SDB. We were given, I believe, all of the notebooks during two different missions, is my memory, that covered a time span that went beyond -- that started before and went beyond the events of Srebrenica, and we were then later also given electronic versions of that same material that, again, went beyond the time-frame that we were most interested in. I cannot say with certainty that we received absolutely all of the information, but I don't have any reason to believe, based on the fact that we were given all of the notebooks, that substantial information was missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: During your testimony in Tolimir, on page 7820, in response to the question whether you were aware that there was a possibility that those intercepts were fabricated or made up or altered in some manner, in the elapsed time, you said: [In English] [As read] "... directly, not specifically during that period of three years but that -- that are -- was a possibility in general, yes." [Interpretation] So how do you know that you were given everything?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Well, I can't say for sure. I mean, you really probably should ask the ABiH. I can't say for sure, but I can tell you that we received, as I just said, all of the notebooks, and the notebooks were the original place where the ABiH recorded, transcribed the conversations. There were no pages missing from those notebooks, and the notebooks covered a period that, again, went far beyond the scope or the range of the events of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just -- there was a quote to Tolimir, at 78:20. Ms. Frease's testimony in Tolimir goes from page 4961 of the transcript through 5336, so I just alert Mr. Karadzic to that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you instructed to take into account the possibility of counterfeiting or minor changes or alterations? So did you receive instructions or orders from your team leaders, or from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. We -- it almost went without saying. We had to be absolutely certain that we could verify the authenticity of the documents and that we then could also consider them to be reliable. So, I mean, our team didn't work on the basis of orders, but certainly communication and agreement - absolute, fundamental agreement - that we needed to answer all questions that we had about the source of the intercepts, the quality of the intercepts, the procedures that were followed in taking them down so that we could be absolutely certain that they were not counterfeits.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you find any instances of counterfeits or alterations? Let's bear that in mind, too. Minor alterations that would affect the actual meaning.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Okay. Counterfeits, I think I've just clarified. We -- we absolutely satisfied ourselves -- I satisfied myself that these intercepts are authentic, genuine, and reliable. The reliability issue goes to your second issue of minor alterations. We did observe in the notebooks that, at times, a word would be crossed out, it would be changed. Sometimes a whole transcript would be crossed out, and the intercept operator would re-transcribe it, after having listened to it again. And then we ran into situations where -- rather, when two or three different operators recorded the same conversation, that they could have picked up the conversation slightly differently so there could have been either slight differences in the way that they transcribed, heard and transcribed the conversation, but I would not say that we found that there were substantive differences in those instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With this example where an entire transcript was crossed out and then re-listened and re-transcribed, how do we know which of those were accurate?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Well, the one that was crossed out would have been considered less accurate. I mean, just like if I'm taking notes here now and cross it out, write something more accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But what would happen if that operator did not -- had not noticed that it wasn't accurate and had just left it as it was?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Well, this went to the procedures that the operators used, the training that they had, the quality of the individuals who were recruited to work there. So they were serious people who were doing a serious job, and they tried to make the transcripts as accurate as they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: From conversations with them and also from listening to tapes, audiotapes, and comparing the audiotapes to the transcripts that they had provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that either MUP -- or, rather, the state security or the BH army were a warring party? One of the warring parties.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you observe any instances that there were lines added, especially in the typewritten form, that were not present in the handwritten notes?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: So you're speaking now specifically of SDB transcripts?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, all transcripts from all sources, both from the SDB source and the BH army source. Did you observe that sometimes they would put forward their position by annotating, making a comment, and especially, did you ever observe that there was something in the type-written form that was not present in the handwritten form?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: So we only -- the SDB did not have handwritten forms -- handwritten notebooks, so it was the military that had the notebooks and then transcribed them. Very, very rarely - but sometimes - there could be examples of where the typist would add something, and I'm just remembering an instance where -- where a typist added something in parentheses about the communication, about the location of the two people communicating, that was not in the original notebook. Because it was in parentheses, it was clear to me, based on conversations with the intercept operators that that was a comment because that was their standard way of indicating that they weren't certain about something. But I cannot, off the top of my head, think of situations where the intercept operators added their own personal analysis or notes in the body of the content.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. But did you then observe that there were any malicious or neutral comments added where the person who was transcribing this was actually behaving as a member of the warring party?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: The only instance that comes to mind would be in the SDB transcripts where their heading on every conversation started off with: The following conversation was intercepted from the aggressor's army. So if that's what you mean by adding a personal view, that would be an example. That's the only example that I can think of. And, of course, the aggressor's army, referring to the VRS; the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have occasion to observe, for instance, that they would say, And then criminal so-and-so picked up the line?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I don't remember that specifically. It's -- it's possible that it could have ended up in a header, but I cannot remember any examples where such a comment would have ended up in the text of the actual intercepted conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that it was possible to establish whether an intercept was accurate. Were you provided all of the audio recordings of intercepts that you analysed in order to be able to check them, check their authenticity?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No, we were not provided all of the audio recordings. And just in the context of the situation at the time, of course, the war was still going on. Supplies were very short. And they taped over conversations continuously. They re-used the reel-to-reel tapes. They didn't have enough tapes to archive all of them, all of the conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of your work, did you ever -- were you ever involved in the same type of work as was the case in -- on this Intercept Project?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Can you clarify your question just a little, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this the first Intercept Project that you ever had to deal with in your entire career.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
