utterances.text: Thank you. In the Popovic case, on page 7824, you stated that it took you a year to gain a better understanding of the process of interception and that you arrived at that point based on interviews with the operators in 1999; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, that sounds right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is the page number correct again?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. I assume -- I haven't looked it up, but probably earlier Mr. Karadzic was referring to the Popovic case rather than Tolimir. This is correct for the Popovic case, 7824.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in the footnote the transcript pages refer to 6.000-something. But let's move on. Footnotes in 92 ter amalgamated statements. I haven't checked it. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's because it was a very long testimony that took place on different dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Because Ms. Frease could come on a testify about a particular topic and then come back later. That's, Your Honour, why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably my memory failed already. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, in a way, you were a beginning in this area -- a beginner in this area.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened with the period of time during that year during which you had lesser understanding of the process; that is to say, prior to your gaining better insight?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I worked on the material with others in the team and just worked through it methodically, notebook by notebook, page by page, matched up various conversations that came. We learned then from different sites, from different units and, in this way, established a very solid knowledge and understanding of the material and the processes that were used to collect it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you then go back to the part of the work you had done during the initial year or did you leave it the way it had been done, although had you less understanding at the time?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Well, the work evolved, so even our methodology evolved. But we constantly incorporated the work that we started off with initially into later work products. So what I mean by that is that when we started to analyse the material, we simply did it on a Excel table, recording the date, the people who were speaking, the people whose names were mentioned in the recordings, locations that were mentioned, and then a small summary. And then we developed a database that we put all of that information into. And in that database, we had fields where we could enter information about the source of that conversation, the format that that conversation came in. So we had one field for a printout, what page it came from, we had another field then added for the notebooks, what notebook number it came from, and the ERN number associated with that particular conversation, the page of that conversation, and that was how the process evolved. So it wasn't that we disregarded everything that we did from the beginning. It was incorporated into our work as we progressed through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us if there's any importance -- or how did it come about that there were changes to single letters, especially in terms of capital letters, in the typed transcripts?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Are you referring to reports that were typed in all capital letters as opposed to those that were typed in a standard sentence structure with a capital letter at the beginning, followed by lower case letters?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. When a text is in capital letters, or sometimes there were texts in the lower case with capital letters at the beginning of words, and then there were cases of mixing both. What I'm trying to get at is whether any significance should be attached to it. Does it have any importance?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. The -- this is a slightly complicated answer. I will just take it bit by bit. The original binder with 550 pages in it contained both conversations that were typed in all caps and others that were typed in standard sentence structure format. We learned later that those that were typed in all caps were conversations take down by the SDB, the police; whereas, the conversations that were typed in standard sentence format were ones that were recorded and typed by the military. When we got to know the process better, we learned that at the northern site where there were both military and police units working that they shared information and forwarded the information to their respective commands. So some of the MUP reports -- the teletype machine, as I understand it, the teletype machine that the MUP had always converted their material to all caps. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If it is the only explanation, then yes. But is there another?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No. Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am slightly confused by your statement that the DB did not have handwritten notes. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look then at P4618. It should not be broadcast as the witness in question was protected, since the witness's handwriting may be recognised. For the other half of the screen, could we have 31036B. Yes, perhaps this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is probably a direct translation of what we have. Since you know our language, can you see that it's a handwritten note and an English translation?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Instead of the English on the right-hand side, could we have 31036B.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look. It's just following the ERN number ending in 600. Can you see that there's a typed remark in brackets that is missing from the handwritten original?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So does it change the meaning of this intercept?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I just ask Mr. Karadzic to clarify. Sorry to go back. Page 50, line 5: "Q. I'm slightly confused by your statement that the DB did not have handwritten notes. Did you say that? "A. Yes, I did ..." And then he brings up this document. Is Dr. Karadzic asserting that this intercept was taken by a DB operative, because that's what the question implies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so. As soon as I have the KDZ number, I will be able to tell you the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can tell you that it was a military unit on the southern site that took this intercept. It wasn't the SDB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And it does correspond to the examples that I was giving about how the typed version that the military provided was in standard sentence structure, not all caps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I think should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the handwriting of Witness KDZ126. I believe he was at the northern location.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I don't have any notes in front of me and I'm going purely off of memory. If I had notes to look at, I could definitely confirm it, but I believe this was from the southern site. I -- I know the names of the two people who were on this intercept, who took it down, and then who -- who typed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Until we found our way in our papers, I wanted to ask you this: Is it true that you said that everything that was handed over was preserved without judging relevance because it could be dealt with later?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: So ... what I understand your question to be is whether everything that we received, we preserved without judging its relevance. If that's what you mean, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So nothing was eliminated, not even the things at the time that seemed unimportant to you. Everything was preserved; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you notice any intercepts which confirm my participation in the critical events you followed?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. My memory is that there were only a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are they at our disposal? Did you hand them over; and did you see them in the material offered by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't think the witness can really speak to the disclosure in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: She can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't speak to the disclosure in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you come across any intercepts of my conversation that would be favourable or unfavorable, for me; that is to say, that would be of use for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I can't remember any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In any case, your team did not keep any intercepts which may have been either in my favour or against me; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: We kept all of the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you rely on your knowledge of Serbian, or Croatian, or our language that is used there, whatever we call it, to deal with turns of phrase, metaphors, and figures of speech? Was it all clear to you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: A lot of it was clear, but where it wasn't, I asked interpreters or language assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The interpreters or language assistants were Serbs? Muslims?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Could have been either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And were they?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: So the majority were Bosnians or Bosnian Muslim, but it depended. Because if they went to the translation unit, then often they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have a problem, for example, with the term "screening," "trijaza"?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I think it was just translated into English as "triage."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So can you tell us what it meant, what connotations it received in the English language?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I know that it comes up in a conversation, I think at 11.11, in discussing prisoners and that triage should be conducted on them, but I've never put my own thoughts or opinions into what that meant. It was -- it was, to my memory, only used once in a conversation and was then later also confirmed through some -- through a document, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The term "packet" is something you have ascribed a specific meaning to. How did you arrive at that meaning?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. Be -- given the context in which that word was used, which was, I believe, Ljuba Beara, the head of security for the VRS Main Staff, saying that he had 6.000 packets that still needed to be delivered. I believe that conversation happened on the 15th of July, and in the context of the events that had occurred and had been occurring, it -- the conclusion was that it referred to people, and I agreed with that conclusion. It was an interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are there other possible interpretations?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I mean, Ljubisa Beara was involved with the prisoners during this entire period. It wasn't, you know, Federal Express or package delivery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since Mr. Karadzic seems to be moving away from the transcript we have in front of us now, I'm putting the question. Did you get any explanation why this passage in the parentheses in the typed version appears, which we can not see in the handwritten version. You understand what I mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The intermediary and Karadzic are sitting in the same room, in the parenthesis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So, no, I don't remember getting a specific explanation on that, but in reading -- reading the transcript, there's certain point in the -- in the transcript where it says ... so there's a parentheses in the transcript and it comes down -- I don't know if you want to look at the English version of it as well. It's the second time that D speaks and it says in parentheses, on the handwritten version, that he can be heard in the background. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's X. Heard in the background.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. X, that's correct. So I -- I think what happened is that when the person was typing this up, he read that and then at the top of the transcript in parentheses put that the intermediary and Karadzic were sitting in the same room. Again, because it is in parentheses, it means it's not something solid, but that would be my best assessment of what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We no longer need this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be useful if you explained to us why in your testimony you use the term "material difference," as opposed to alterations, changes, inaccuracies. Could another legal term be used for material difference, and what would be the appropriate term to use instead?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I really try not to use legal terms in my testimony. So I would just say not a substantial difference. I may have used material difference before, but it would just mean something that substantively changed the meaning of the content.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that -- for example, the previous document, which implies that I was in the same room with the intermediary who could hear Deronjic, which, in other words, would mean that I could hear him too, is something that did not change the meaning, the remark itself?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It didn't change the substance of the conversation. It made the context a little confusing. But the intermediary was probably holding two phones and passing messages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, that sentence stating that I'm sitting next to him completely changes the picture; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Well, again, it's in parentheses. So the operators were told always to put things in parentheses if they weren't sure about something. So another example would be where someone was very familiar with one particular person's voice but that particular person's name had not been mentioned in the conversation. So they would put X, but then, in parentheses, they would probably put that person's name to provide some context. So we wouldn't take the material in parentheses to be absolutely concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony in Popovic, page 7882, you explained this term "material difference," saying you used that term to denote differences conducive to a change of meaning; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's possible. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, in court, there would be a more appropriate term for that, wouldn't there? [In English] Tampered, or fabricated, or altered, or what would you prefer?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree with those terms. Certainly not tampered or fabricated. Depends -- the context that we're talking about are substantial differences in the meaning of something, and that doesn't necessarily mean that something was fabricated or tampered with. There could be lot of other explanations for it, like the one I just gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll come to that. If the operator doesn't hear properly and such, but could we agree that such a document is unusable or of limited use in court if the meaning has been changed?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I think it's most useful to talk about specific examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We don't have time, Ms. Frease. I would like to know your position. You, yourself, spoke of material difference, things that changed the meaning, and you work for the court; more precisely for the Office of the Prosecutor. What is your position?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Well, I think it's -- from the standpoint of an operator who was listening to these conversations day in and day out, if that person did not hear a particular part of a conversation, the honest thing and what they did was that they didn't put anything. They put three dots or "inaudible" or something like that. So if the operator didn't hear properly, I can't agree with the statement that such a document is unusable. It simply means that they weren't able to capture the entire conversation for technical reasons, but it doesn't invalidate the parts of the conversation that they were able to capture.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see Mr. Nicholls on his feet, but I would like to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. Page 57, line 19: "You, yourself, spoke of material differences, things that change the meaning." In the cite at page 7882 of Popovic we had earlier, on cross-examination, Ms. Frease was asked to define what she meant by the term "material differences." The question as phrased as -- if Mr. Karadzic is asserting the witness, Ms. Frease, said she had found material differences that changed the meaning, I want a cite, please, because that's the way question is phrased, "You, yourself, spoke of material differences ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And whether it is useable or unusable for the -- for the Court, and what probative value to be assessed, it's... yeah. With the Court and what probative value to be assessed by the Court. It is for the Chamber. It's nothing -- it's nothing to do with the witness. So this whole exercise is -- is a bit pointless, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Frease, I began with the question why you used the euphemism "material difference" instead of a legal term, any legal term, because you are working for the judiciary? Is it true that also in Popovic, on the next page, you were unable to identify the scope of alterations that would constitute a material difference? Would you be able to tell us now what scale of alteration causes such a difference that would -- that would disserve a legal term, whether the change was deliberate or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us see the page, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Also, just want to correct at line [sic] 59. The witness is not working for the judiciary, and the witness has explained why she tries not to use legal terms, because she's no lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting, Ms. Frease, is the date on the intercept important, in terms of accuracy? Would a wrong date constitute a material difference?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, it could. We paid very close attention to dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And would the hour of the intercept also be important, in terms of forensic use?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is probably the right document, but we are now looking for the number. My number was 7882. I don't know if it's the same here in e-court. Did you notice passages or words crossed out, the time, the hour and minute crossed out? Did you come across cases where an earlier transcript would appear later in chronology?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It would be helpful if you could try to use a specific example. I can maybe try to speak to one of the issues in terms of an hour, a minute being crossed out. I remember there being an issue about zeros having a line through them, there being discussion about that. That was how some operators wrote their numbers. In terms of passages or words being crossed out, we discussed that briefly, and that happened sometimes when the operators would go back and listen to the conversation again. Things would become more clear and so they would correct their work product.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you to cast a glance at this page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this the dialogue in the courtroom in the Popovic case; and are these your words?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what passage do you -- do you refer to, Mr. Karadzic? This is part of cross-examination, I take it, by Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And I would now like us to focus on the passage beginning with the line 4, when Mr. Ostojic is trying to establish the nature of the term "material difference." And further below, Ms. Frease is saying what would and what would not constitute "material difference."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm fairly consistent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, did she say that she found material difference in this sense?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is probably examination-in-chief -- sorry. This is a reference to the examination-in-chief. And it says she had used the term the day before, the term "material difference" describing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You need to show her where she referred to "material difference." It says page 69 at the time, but could you find the correct page, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm looking, Your Honour. I'm trying to, but I haven't found it yet because I can't search it electronically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is whether, Ms. Frease, these added words, terms, criminal and others, changed dates, wrong dates, inconsistencies in chronology, later intercepts appearing earlier, et cetera, would all that, in her view, be a material difference that changes the meaning? And I don't care what she found about that and what she stated in the Popovic case, but I want to hear her position here and now.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: More precisely, Ms. Frease, what is the threshold that you set above which something has been so substantially changed that it changes meaning?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I guess that's part of the point. We just didn't find that. You know, there could have been human errors. You know, human mistakes. Not hearing a word properly. I'm not even sure you call that a mistake. But you don't hearing something properly so you write down one thing, one name instead of another name. But we just did not find substantial mistakes or changes or anything in this material that caused us alarm, that caused us to doubt it. And when you speak of dates being incorrect, I -- I would take issue with that. When you speak of there being inconsistency in chronology I would like you to be specific about the inconsistencies in chronology. I can give you an example of how that could happen. But these are all issues that can be explained and that do not have anything in the -- in the work that I did, in the conversations that I had with people, in all of the conversations that we had within the team, in the comparisons that we made, with many other sources of information, we did not find substantial differences, substantial problems, in the intercepts that changed, radically changed, the meaning of a particular intercept.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, could we have a shorter break today because I would finish within half an hour after the break. We don't have to have a long day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You -- let me understood you correctly: You need about half an hour to conclude your cross-examination and you'd like to conclude as early as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any problem on the part of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Frankly, I haven't yet decided if I have any re-direct. It would be brief. But I may have a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But there would be no problem in having a half an hour break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I'd like to confirm with the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have a --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question on this topic while it's still fresh.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that if you encountered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, let's have a break. And, in the meantime, we'll find the passage where she referred to the material difference, and let's deal with it then. We'll have a break for half an hour. We resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just very quickly at page 53, line 4, I think there's an -- or there is an error in the transcript. It says "can"; the word "can." I think it clearly was "can't." And, second, the passage in the previous day referred to by Mr. Ostojic in the Popovic testimony is from the 26th of February, 2007, page 7995 where Ms. Frease is answering a question which begins on 7794.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. In page 7882, Mr. Ostojic referred to material difference that Ms. Frease mentioned, so the page number should precede that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I said it wrong. It's 7795.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know the e-court page? Why don't you upload it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I think it should be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It just may be best to show the previous page so the question is intelligible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Bottom, probably. Bottom of page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So for our record, I will read out ... Let us read out the passage. It is Mr. Vanderpuye's question: "Could I ask you just to evaluate the differences that you found. Did you find that ..." Next page: "... the import of the conversations had changed in any way as a result of those differences? In other words, was the conversation materially affected, in your mind, based upon those differences? " And witness's answer was: "I can't think of any -- where I thought there was a material difference." That's the context she referred -- referred to material difference, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, and what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is: Do you believe that this note that I'm sitting together with the intermediary is legally important or not? Does it change my legal position or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's not for her to answer, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Excellencies, before that ever comes to the table of the Trial Chamber, this legal team worked on it and their job is described as collecting, assembling and analysing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your question was does it change your legal position or not. That's for the Chamber to assess, and you can make submission on that. She gave her -- the -- the evaluation as -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did that team notice it and notify anyone that there is a difference, or did they judge that it doesn't matter? The question here is: Did the team make judgements that should have been left to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: no. That's -- whether the team noticed -- notified anyone, that is different. That's a separate question. But your question was formulated in such a manner that it's impossible for the witness to answer, I thought.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want the witness to state clearly did they make assessments as to what constitutes an important material difference. Based on what did they make those judgements? And I'm citing an example where, I believe, they should have noticed the difference and notified it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is the question: Did you notice the difference, and did you warn the users of your services that it exists?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It's been a number of years since I've worked on this material, but I believe that we would have seen the difference because we compared the written conversations to the typed conversations, but the explanation that we came up with was the one that I gave previously, which was that X in the typewritten conversation had noted that -- now I don't have it in front of me, but that both the intermediary and Karadzic were in the same room -- or, not in the same room, that they could both be heard, I think is what that original transcription said. And then when the person typed it up, they put in parentheses that both people were in the same room. So that was a hypothesis. Which, frankly, should not have been added. But, again, because it was in parentheses, it was not something that we considered to be -- to change the meaning of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is what I want to know. Did you decide what changes meaning? Did you have, by your side, a lawyer whom you could consult?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: We had a team lawyer, definitely. We talked about this material and other issues continuously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you consult him on this specific example, on this specific case, whether the difference is substantial?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I do not have a specific memory of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move to another subject. We had already started to discuss this. Do you agree that pages, dates, times, and chronology of intercepts should be established accurately, precisely?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Those are different issues that you raise, and I'm happy to take them one at a time. So for the issue of dates, dates were critical. And where we were uncertain of dates, we indicated that until we could confirm them. Times were also important, but they were more difficult for us to -- to confirm, except when we had the same conversation that was recorded two or three times by different operators. And in those instances, the times were self-reinforcing. I've discussed in the past why the conversations would have been off by a minute, or two minutes, or five minutes, and that simply had to do with the time that each operator saw on his watch or the clock on the wall. So times -- those sorts of time differences would not have been considered significant. In fact, to the contrary. I would say they reinforced reliability of the intercepts. As to the chronology and the timing of the chronology of the intercepts, which I think is what you're getting at, on some of the printed material, you will see that some of the intercepts are out of a time chronology. That is, that you could see -- you might see one conversation that starts -- or a series of conversations that start at 1.00 in the afternoon, carry through to 3.00, and then you might see a conversation interspersed that, say, was from 2.00, and then they might continue on after 3.00. So the question would be: Why was that conversation from 2.00 in the middle of the other conversations? And the answer to that is that it's possible that a notebook could have been handed over to a typist to be typed in the interim, especially if the intercept operator who took that conversation at 2.00 thought it was important. So he could have just handed it over to the typist and said, Hey, fit this one in. You know, It should go now. And then take -- took the notebook back and then the typist continued with the notebook that he had. So that's an explanation for why, in some of the printout versions of the intercept transcripts, you see times that may not run in a perfect sequence or chronology.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that the only explanation? You said "possible," "a possible explanation." So is that the only explanation?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It's the only one that I can think of right now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 65 ter 35036, please. That's notebook 99. Could we pull that up in e-court, please. Can we have page 1046.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, could you just look at this cover page. What date appears there? It says, "As of 16 July 1995"; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm actually not sure. 16 ... I don't know if that's a 7. Looks like an 8 or a 5. The interior page says the 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, on the cover page, it says the 16th; correct? More specifically, it says, "As of the 16th." And this is most probably July. It's impossible that it could be anything else. So we see that it is as of the 16th; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. So some of the ways when we were first working with the notebooks that we dated conversations was by counting backwards or forwards and trying to determine which conversations would have taken place on particular days. There often were not dates within notebooks consistently. So it looks like, in this one, the date of the 19th appears on page 27, and then we counted backwards to the beginning of the notebook. And those days would have -- the times within those days would have run chronologically so that you could tell when the next day began. We would have considered the date of the 19th to have been a firm date. If there was another date, say, later in the notebook, of the 21st, and the in-between times ran sequentially from morning to night, or afternoon to night and into the next day, then we would have considered the 20th to have also been a firm date. With this one, it would be helpful if I could see it, actually physically, but I'm not sure that we would have considered those other dates, even if we counted backwards to the 16th, to have been firm dates, based on the cover of the notebook. We would have relied upon other information to confirm when those conversations took place. So our very simple system of determining what an approximate date was and what a firm date was, was whether or not the date was bolded. So it gave us an orientation, it gave us a sort of idea of when we thought it happened, but we didn't consider it firm until we had other ways of corroborating those dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please note lines 11 and 12. In 12 you say -- on line 12, you say, "It could still be the 17th." utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we can go back to the document we saw a little earlier, 35036 on the 65 ter list. Now, did you note that under the 19th of July, in the 19th of July area, there was a date that was crossed out in red ink; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.text: Do you know who paid for the engagement of Mr. Hunter?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But if you knew where this Commander Gengo, who is mentioned here below, you would know that that is the same area. Can we agree that it's the 11th May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show this part, the header.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be marked as -- for identification as D2209. In the meantime, Mr. Karadzic, you used all of your time, three hours. Do you have more? And I --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's just finish with this notebook and the date, 19 July. I have just one more question and I'll be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we put that notebook on the ELMO, that page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I look at it first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe the ERN is 1484, if this has ERN numbers at all. But the date is 19 July. Maybe that way we can find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So if you have found the page, could you put it on the ELMO so that we can take a look as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Do you want me to hold it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So did the red line refer to that long line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. So a new day beginning, the 19th. And a couple of ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, continue, Ms. Frease.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A couple of pages later on this same day there is more red ink here. And here. And here. So it was an intercept operator who wanted to establish when the 19th began, and so he just took his pen and lined there and marked the date of the 19th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And that line was visible in photocopy as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apparently it wasn't. Because I didn't see it on the screen. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think I saw it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh. Really?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry. Shall we upload the notebook? 1D -- no. 35036.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I would also say that I can now, when I see the original, I can see that this is a 7. 16.7. It's not -- to me it's not clear on the original -- or, on it's photocopy as it is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is clearly visible in the e-court as well, in the photocopy, that line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The red line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The read line, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, so it is. I don't know what I was looking at before, but I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Your Honours it's just the question back at page 75, line 17, said: Is it correct you confirmed that the date the 19th of July had been crossed out in red ink? And this is a line we're looking at the book. He said it's a start of a date, so to me, it's just slightly different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I don't remember how the Popovic transcript read. But, Mr. Karadzic, having seen this original, do you like to ask any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question would only be why it's in a different colour and why she accepted in the Popovic case that it was crossed out in red. Because she claimed it was crossed out in red.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: My explanation for why it's in red is that a few pages - one, two - five pages later, there -- intercept operator is writing in red ink on the next three pages in total in red. So I don't -- I don't know why I would have agreed that the date was crossed out. It -- it's not crossed out. It's -- there's a line, and the date is put below that line to indicate a new day is beginning. So I don't know whether I was not able -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When is it indicated that it's the beginning of a new day? When is this indication in red made? Because both below the line and above the line, it's the same writing, in the same pen. And then the next day's entry is in a different pen, the same pen used three or four days earlier. Did you ask for an explanation of this? Who made the -- who put in the date? Because the person who wrote in blue is not the same as the one who wrote in red.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: May I have the transcript now back up on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, Popovic transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the current one so I can see what the questions are. Okay. So when -- your question, "When is it indicated that it's the beginning of a new day?" It's indicated by the fact that there's a line drawn across and the date written down as the 19th of July, 1995. The conversation, the previous conversation was recorded at 2341. The conversation following the date of the 19th of July was recorded at 6.25 in the morning. So it was -- the previous conversation was the end of one day and it's next conversation was the beginning of a new day. And then -- I disagree that it's the same handwriting above and below the line. Those are two different operators that are writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I said the same pen, blue pen which we can't see on the copy. It's the same colour. And then, at some point later, the same pen that was used four or five pages later, was used to put in this date. Do you agree that it was not written in the same go. It was inserted at some later point in the same colour as used by the -- by the writer four, five pages later. You can see that better on the original.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I can't say that it was the same blue pen that was written -- that an operator used at 2341 and at 0625 in the morning. But, yes, a red pen was used five or six pages later, because it looks like his black pen had run out of ink so he picked up a red pen and continued the conversation in red ink and then went back and said because that conversation, the first conversation, that is written in red ink starts at 10.32 in the morning on the same day. So then that person would have just gone back and drawn a line and put the day's date in, realising that the date had not been recorded for that day. And then various other operators also used that red pen in a few subsequent conversations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now, it's time for you to conclude, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My last question, Ms. Frease. Have you ever put the paper to expertise to determine the age of the paper, along with a graphology expertise, analysis of the log-book; in other words, did any independent institution outside the Office of the Prosecutor analyse all these elements?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: To my knowledge, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies, for your patience and understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Frease, for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably to understand the context of this part of what witness -- probably we need to admit the relevant page of that notebook; in particular, in colour. That can be done, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And it's -- it's not a huge document. I'd suggest we colour scan the whole -- the whole notebook and put it in for the purposes of understanding the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. In that context, shall we give the number for the notebook? As a Defence exhibit. It's not in evidence yet, the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe not. Well, I may be wrong. There was one notebook that we put in as a demonstrative, but I don't recall whether it was this one, off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll give a number for that. But we don't need the translation we just admit it to see the colour, or -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be assigned Exhibit D2210. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. Do it now or after a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. It's -- I think we had -- given that we had only half an hour break it now that we should adjourn for the day. But if it is not that lengthy then we, with the indulgence of the interpreters yet again, can continue for some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I will ask one question or maybe two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll make it shorter. P00140, please. This is an intercept from 14 July 1995 at 2102 hours. That's right. If I could have the English, please. I believe we're looking at version A for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, are you familiar with this intercept --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please also see the manuscript on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's on its way, I take it. Yes, let us continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was asking if you're familiar with this intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. We talk about it before. Palma is which headquarters?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know who Major Jokic is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Dragan Jokic ... I can't come up with his title right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: He was a duty officer at some point. Oh, well, there he says duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And Badem, do you remember who -- which headquarters Badem is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, that's Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: First line, it says: "Hello, Badem, let me talk to Beara." Do you know Colonel Beara is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, he was the head of security for the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we look down on the English, keeping in mind this is the 14th of July. If we look down further, we say under -- we say -- we see Jokic saying: "Yes, hey, we have huge problems over here." I'm moving quickly. This is before Beara has come on the line. And then Jokic says: "There were big problems, well, with the people. I mean, with the parcel."

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Are you aware of what the situation was in Zvornik regarding prisoners of war on the 14th July in the evening?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What was it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It was that thousands were being held in various places and being executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In this context, having the research we've talked about and Mr. Karadzic showed you a tonne of documents with paket or parcel, what would you take parcel to mean here?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Unless my colleagues have questions for, that concludes your evidence, Ms. Frease.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On behalf of the Tribunal I would to thank you for coming to The Hague to give it again. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought to ask -- the witness mentioned 6.000 packages. I never found that anywhere. And perhaps Mr. Nicholls could be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a separate intercept, I take it. Now you are free to go, but it is time to adjourn for the day so we rise all together. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've been asked to address two quick housekeeping matters. The first is with respect to the ICMP funding doc, no problem. The second is with respect to the Defence request for the presence of Mr. Paselic as a demographic expert. We were awaiting the CV. Again, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be given a number. And one further thing. On 9th of March, Prosecution informed us that it has uploaded into e-court a public redacted version of Exhibit P276 under the 65 ter 14691A as ordered by the Chamber in the decision of 2nd of March, 2012. And so the Chamber is now satisfied that its order has been complied with and requests the Registry to assign an exhibit number to that document. Then, with that, we'll adjourn for the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 26th day of March, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.
